question: What are the common symptoms of fever?
answer: A fever means your body temperature is higher than normal, usually 38 C (100.4 F) or above. It is often a sign that the body is fighting an infection. Common signs are feeling hot, sweating, chills and shivering, headache, muscle aches, tiredness, loss of appetite and mild dehydration. Rest, drink plenty of fluids, wear light clothing and keep the room comfortable. Ask a pharmacist or doctor which fever medicine is suitable for you. See a doctor if the fever lasts more than 3 days, goes above 39.5 C (103 F), or comes with a stiff neck, rash, confusion, trouble breathing or severe pain.

question: What causes headaches?
answer: Most headaches are tension-type headaches or migraines and are not dangerous. Common triggers include stress, dehydration, missed meals, poor sleep, eye strain and too much screen time. Tension headaches feel like a tight band around the head. Migraines are often one-sided, throbbing, and may come with nausea or sensitivity to light and sound. Rest in a quiet dark room, drink water, eat regular meals, sleep well, take screen breaks and manage stress. Keep a diary to find your triggers. Get urgent medical help for a sudden very severe headache, headache after a head injury, or headache with fever and stiff neck, confusion, weakness or vision changes.

question: What are the symptoms of the common cold?
answer: The common cold is a mild viral infection of the nose and throat. It usually gets better by itself in 7 to 10 days. Typical symptoms are a runny or blocked nose, sneezing, sore throat, mild cough, mild headache and feeling tired. Allergies cause similar sneezing but usually no fever and last longer. Rest, drink warm fluids, use steam inhalation or salt-water nasal rinses, and wash hands often to avoid spreading it. Antibiotics do not work against colds. See a doctor if symptoms last more than 10 days, you have a high fever, ear or chest pain, trouble breathing, or if a baby, older adult or person with a chronic illness is affected.

question: What precautions should be taken when taking medicine?
answer: Medicines are safe when used correctly. Always follow the instructions from your doctor or pharmacist and read the label before use. Check the dose, timing and expiry date. Tell your doctor about allergies, other medicines, supplements and pregnancy. Never share prescription medicines with others. Do not stop or change a prescribed medicine on your own, store medicines away from children, and ask a pharmacist before combining medicines. Contact a doctor or pharmacist if you get a rash, swelling, trouble breathing, vomiting or any unusual reaction. For a suspected overdose, call emergency services right away.

question: When should antibiotics be used?
answer: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections only. They do not work against viruses such as the common cold or flu. Using antibiotics when they are not needed, or stopping early, can cause antibiotic resistance. Side effects can include stomach upset, diarrhoea and allergic reactions. Take antibiotics only when prescribed, finish the course exactly as your doctor says, and never use leftover antibiotics. See a doctor if you get a rash, swelling of the face, trouble breathing, severe diarrhoea, or if you do not improve after a few days of treatment.

question: What should I do if I have severe chest pain?
answer: Severe chest pain can be a sign of a heart attack and is a medical emergency. Call your local emergency number (for example 112 or 108 in India, 911 in the US) immediately. Warning signs include pressure or tightness in the chest, pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back, shortness of breath, cold sweat, nausea and light-headedness. Stop all activity and sit down, stay calm, and unlock your door if you are alone. Do not drive yourself to hospital. If a doctor has told you to, chew an aspirin while waiting for help. Call emergency services immediately. Do not wait to see if the pain goes away.

question: What should I do if someone is choking?
answer: Choking is an emergency when a person cannot cough, speak or breathe. Call emergency services immediately. Signs are being unable to speak or cry, a silent or weak cough, clutching the throat and blue lips. For an adult or child over 1 year: encourage coughing; if they cannot cough, give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, and repeat until help arrives. For a baby, use back blows and chest thrusts only. Learning first aid in a certified course is very helpful. Call emergency services immediately. Anyone who needed abdominal thrusts should be checked by a doctor afterwards.

question: What are the symptoms of high blood pressure?
answer: High blood pressure (hypertension) usually has no symptoms, which is why it is called the silent killer. Over time it raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease. Reduce salt, stay active, maintain a healthy weight, limit alcohol, avoid smoking, manage stress and check your pressure regularly. See a doctor for regular high readings. Seek emergency care for very high pressure with chest pain, severe headache, weakness or trouble speaking.

Good choices are leafy greens, colourful vegetables, fruit, whole grains like oats and brown rice, pulses, nuts, seeds, fish, eggs, dairy or alternatives, and olive or mustard oil in small amounts. Fill half your plate with vegetables and fruit, eat regular meals, control portion sizes, drink water instead of sugary drinks and cook at home when you can. Talk to a doctor or dietitian if you have diabetes, kidney disease, food allergies, are pregnant, or want to make big changes to your diet.

question: How much water should I drink in a day?
answer: Water helps control body temperature, digestion, joints and kidney function. Most healthy adults need around 2 to 3 litres of fluids a day, more in hot weather or when exercising. Signs of dehydration are thirst, dry mouth, dark yellow urine, headache, tiredness, dizziness and passing less urine. Sip water through the day, eat fruit and vegetables with high water content, and drink more when it is hot or when you are ill. Pale yellow urine is a good sign. See a doctor if you cannot keep fluids down, feel very dizzy or confused, or pass very little urine. People with heart or kidney disease should ask how much to drink.

question: What are the benefits of regular exercise?
answer: Regular exercise strengthens the heart, muscles and bones, helps control weight and improves mood and sleep. It lowers the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, some cancers and depression, and improves energy, balance and memory. Adults should aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, such as brisk walking, plus muscle-strengthening exercise on 2 days. Start slowly and increase gradually. Check with a doctor before starting if you have heart disease, chest pain, dizziness, joint problems, are pregnant or have been inactive for a long time.

question: Why is getting enough sleep important?
answer: Sleep lets the body repair itself, strengthens the immune system and helps memory, learning and mood. Most adults need 7 to 9 hours a night. Long-term lack of sleep increases the risk of obesity, diabetes, heart disease, depression and accidents, and reduces concentration and immunity. Keep a regular sleep schedule, avoid screens and caffeine before bed, keep the bedroom dark and quiet, and get daylight and exercise during the day. See a doctor if you stay very sleepy during the day, snore loudly with pauses in breathing, or sleep problems last for weeks.

question: How can I sleep better at night?
answer: Insomnia means trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early. Stress, irregular routines, caffeine, screen use and some health conditions are common causes. Short-term insomnia often follows stress or a change in routine. Long-term insomnia may be linked to anxiety, depression, pain, sleep apnoea or certain medicines. Go to bed and wake up at the same time daily, avoid caffeine in the afternoon, put phones away an hour before bed, keep the room cool and dark, and try relaxation or breathing exercises. See a doctor if poor sleep lasts more than a few weeks or affects your daytime life. Do not rely on sleeping pills without medical advice.

question: What are the symptoms of flu?
answer: Flu (influenza) is a viral infection of the nose, throat and lungs. It starts suddenly and feels worse than a common cold. Symptoms are fever, chills, cough, sore throat, runny nose, muscle and body aches, headache and tiredness. It usually lasts about a week. Rest, drink plenty of fluids, stay at home to avoid spreading it, cover coughs and wash hands often. A yearly flu vaccine lowers your risk. See a doctor if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or symptoms that improve and then return. Older adults, pregnant women and people with chronic illness should seek early advice.

question: What are the symptoms of food poisoning?
answer: Food poisoning is an illness from eating food or water contaminated with germs. It usually settles in 1 to 3 days. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, watery diarrhoea, mild fever and tiredness. Dehydration is the main danger. Sip oral rehydration solution or clean water often, rest, and eat bland foods like rice, banana or toast when you feel able. Avoid alcohol and oily food. See a doctor if there is blood in the stool, high fever, signs of dehydration, symptoms lasting more than 3 days, or if the patient is a baby, an older adult or pregnant.

Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, watery diarrhoea, mild fever and tiredness. Dehydration is the main danger. Sip oral rehydration solution or clean water often, rest, and eat bland foods like rice, banana or toast when you feel able. Avoid alcohol and oily food. See a doctor if there is blood in the stool, high fever, signs of dehydration, symptoms lasting more than 3 days, or if the patient is a baby, an older adult or pregnant.

question: What causes toothache?
answer: Toothache is most often caused by tooth decay (cavities), but gum disease, a cracked tooth, an abscess or teeth grinding can also cause it. Rinse with warm salt water, brush gently, floss to remove trapped food, and avoid very hot, cold or sugary foods until you see a dentist. See a dentist soon. Seek urgent care for facial swelling, fever, or trouble swallowing or breathing.

See a dentist if gums bleed for more than a week, are swollen or painful, or if you have constant bad breath or loose teeth.

question: How can I reduce eye strain from screens?
answer: Digital eye strain comes from long periods of screen use and causes tired, dry or aching eyes, blurred vision and headaches. We blink less when looking at screens, which dries the eyes. Poor lighting, glare and uncorrected vision problems make it worse. Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes look at something 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds. Blink often, adjust screen brightness and keep the screen at arm's length. Have an eye test if symptoms continue, or if you notice blurred vision, double vision or trouble seeing at night. Most adults should have an eye check every 1 to 2 years.

question: What are common symptoms of anemia?
answer: Anaemia means the blood has too few healthy red blood cells or too little haemoglobin to carry oxygen around the body. Common symptoms are tiredness, weakness, pale skin, dizziness, headache, shortness of breath, cold hands and feet and a fast heartbeat. Iron deficiency is the most common cause. Eat iron-rich foods such as leafy greens, pulses, eggs, meat, dates and fortified cereals, and add vitamin C foods like lemon or orange to help absorption. See a doctor for a blood test to find the cause before taking iron tablets. Seek urgent care for chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness.

question: What causes high cholesterol?
answer: Cholesterol is a fatty substance in the blood. Too much LDL (bad) cholesterol can build up in the arteries and raise the risk of heart attack and stroke. High cholesterol usually has no symptoms and is found by a blood test. Causes include an unhealthy diet, lack of exercise, obesity, smoking, diabetes and family history. Eat more vegetables, fruit, oats, pulses and nuts, cut down on fried food, fatty meat and butter, stay active, stop smoking and keep a healthy weight. Ask your doctor for a cholesterol test, especially if you are over 40 or have diabetes, high blood pressure or a family history of heart disease.

question: Why do I feel dizzy when I stand up?
answer: Dizziness has many causes, including dehydration, low blood sugar, low blood pressure, standing up too quickly, anaemia, ear problems, anxiety and some medicines. Vertigo is a spinning feeling, often from an inner-ear problem. Light-headedness feels like you might faint and is often linked to blood pressure, blood sugar or fluids. Sit or lie down, drink water, eat something, and stand up slowly. Avoid driving or climbing until it passes. Get emergency help if dizziness comes with chest pain, fainting, trouble speaking, weakness, severe headache or vision changes. See a doctor if it keeps coming back.

question: Why do I feel tired all the time?
answer: Feeling tired all the time can come from poor sleep, stress, an unbalanced diet, lack of exercise or an underlying problem such as anaemia, thyroid disease, diabetes or depression. Other causes include infections, vitamin D or B12 deficiency, sleep apnoea, certain medicines and long-term illnesses. Sleep 7 to 9 hours, eat regular balanced meals, drink water, exercise lightly, limit caffeine and alcohol and find time to relax. See a doctor if tiredness lasts more than 2 weeks, or comes with weight loss, fever, shortness of breath, low mood or other new symptoms. Basic blood tests can help find the cause.

question: What should I do for a minor burn?
answer: For a minor burn, cool the area right away under cool running water for 20 minutes. Remove rings or tight items near the burn before swelling starts. Do not use ice, butter, toothpaste or oil, and do not burst blisters. After cooling, cover the burn loosely with a clean non-stick dressing or cling film, keep it clean and dry, and watch for signs of infection. Get medical help for burns larger than your palm, on the face, hands, feet or genitals, deep or white or charred burns, chemical or electrical burns, and burns on babies or older adults.

question: How do I treat a minor cut?
answer: To treat a minor cut, first wash your hands, then press a clean cloth firmly on the wound for several minutes to stop bleeding. Rinse the wound with clean running water, gently clean around it with soap, and cover it with a clean bandage. Change the dressing daily. Keep the wound clean and dry and check that your tetanus vaccination is up to date. For a nosebleed, sit forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for 10 minutes. Get medical care if bleeding does not stop after 10 minutes of pressure, the cut is deep or gaping, caused by an animal bite or dirty object, or shows redness, pus or fever. Call emergency services for heavy bleeding.

question: What are common symptoms of menstrual cramps?
answer: Menstrual cramps are throbbing or aching pains in the lower abdomen that start just before or during a period. They are very common. They can spread to the lower back and thighs and may come with nausea, loose stools, headache and tiredness. They are caused by the womb contracting. A warm heat pad, gentle exercise, rest, warm drinks and relaxation can help. Ask a doctor or pharmacist about suitable pain relief. See a doctor if the pain is severe, gets worse over time, stops you from doing daily activities, comes with very heavy bleeding, or starts after age 25.

question: What are the early signs of pregnancy?
answer: A missed period is often the first sign of pregnancy. Other early signs include tender breasts, nausea, tiredness and needing to pass urine more often. You may also notice mood changes, food cravings or dislikes and mild cramping. A home pregnancy test is most reliable from the first day of a missed period. If pregnant, start folic acid as advised by your doctor, eat a balanced diet, avoid alcohol and smoking, and attend regular antenatal check-ups. Book an appointment to confirm pregnancy. Seek urgent care for heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, fever, or reduced baby movements later in pregnancy.

question: What should I do if a child has a fever?
answer: Fever in children is common and is usually caused by a viral infection. Keep the child comfortable, rested and well hydrated. Dress the child in light clothes, offer plenty of fluids or breast milk and check their temperature. Never give aspirin to children. Ask a doctor or pharmacist about the right medicine and dose for the child's age and weight. Watch how the child is behaving: drinking, playing and responding normally is a good sign. Do not use cold baths or alcohol rubs. Take a baby under 3 months to a doctor straight away for any fever of 38 C (100.4 F) or higher. See a doctor if a child has fever for more than 3 days, a rash, stiff neck, seizure, trouble breathing, refuses to drink, or is very drowsy.

question: How can older adults reduce their risk of falling?
answer: Falls are a leading cause of injury in older adults, but most can be prevented with simple steps. Common causes are weak muscles, poor balance, poor eyesight, some medicines, low blood pressure and hazards at home such as loose rugs, poor lighting and wet floors. Stay active with balance and strength exercises like walking or tai chi, remove loose rugs, add good lighting and grab bars, wear non-slip footwear, and have eyesight and medicines reviewed regularly. See a doctor after any fall, especially if there is a head injury, severe pain or confusion. Call emergency services for loss of consciousness or if the person cannot move.

question: What causes back pain?
answer: Most back pain comes from muscle strain, poor posture, long hours of sitting or lifting heavy objects, and usually improves within a few weeks. Other causes include disc problems, arthritis and, less often, infections or other illnesses. Pain that spreads down the leg may be sciatica. Stay gently active instead of bed rest, use heat packs, sit with back support, take movement breaks every 30 minutes, strengthen your core and lift with your knees. See a doctor if pain lasts more than 4 to 6 weeks, or comes with leg weakness, numbness, fever or weight loss. Get emergency help for loss of bladder or bowel control, or pain after a serious fall.

Acne is caused by blocked oil glands and hormone changes. Allergic rashes are often itchy and red with raised bumps. Infections may be painful, warm or have pus. Dry skin looks flaky and feels tight. Avoid scratching and known triggers, use mild soap, moisturise regularly, wear loose cotton clothes, keep skin clean and do not squeeze pimples. question: What causes joint pain?
answer: Joint pain is often caused by injury, overuse or arthritis. Osteoarthritis is wear and tear of the joints and is common with age, while rheumatoid arthritis is an immune condition. Signs of arthritis include pain, stiffness (especially in the morning), swelling and reduced movement. Extra body weight puts more strain on the knees and hips. Keep moving with low-impact exercise like walking, swimming or cycling, maintain a healthy weight, use heat or cold packs, and eat enough calcium and vitamin D for bone health. See a doctor if a joint is hot, red and swollen, pain lasts more than a few weeks, stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes in the morning, or you cannot move the joint.

question: What are the symptoms of a urinary tract infection?
answer: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is a bacterial infection of the bladder or urinary tract. It is common, especially in women, and needs treatment from a doctor. Symptoms include burning when passing urine, needing to go often, cloudy or strong-smelling urine, lower tummy pain and sometimes blood in the urine. Drink plenty of water, do not hold urine for long, urinate after sex, wipe from front to back and keep the genital area clean. See a doctor for a urine test and treatment. Get urgent care for fever, shaking, back or side pain, vomiting, or if you are pregnant or the patient is a child or older adult.

question: How should I wash my hands properly?
answer: Washing your hands with soap and clean water is one of the best ways to prevent illness. Wet your hands, lather with soap including backs of hands, between fingers and under nails, scrub for at least 20 seconds, rinse well and dry with a clean towel. Wash before eating or cooking, after using the toilet, after coughing or sneezing, after touching animals or rubbish, and after caring for someone sick. Use an alcohol-based sanitizer (at least 60 percent alcohol) when soap is not available. See a doctor if frequent washing causes painful cracked skin or rashes on your hands.
